To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
memory B cells provide an archive of past immune responses, and that the B cell memory repertoire is broader than the circulating antibody repertoire.

memory B cell (BMem) responses to the CD4 binding site and CD4 induced epitopes of HIV-1 envelope are present at high frequencies in the memory B cell pool but are not detected in plasma, and these findings suggest that the BMem pool provides a more comprehensive picture of humoral immunity than plasma antibody (Ab).
the BMem pool provides a more comprehensive picture of Ab specificity than does the plasma Ab repertoire.
In summary, our research is concerned with
understanding the nature of HIV-1-specific B cell immunity in the setting of natural virus control.
the development of a new vaccine strategy to prevent the acquisition of HIV-1.
understanding the immune response of HIV-1 infection, and the development of a vaccine that can elicit a protective response.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
plasma antibody responses are a subset of those found in BMem.
BMem are more likely to be representative of Ab responses than plasma Ab titers.
the B cell compartment in HIV-1-infected individuals contains a large repertoire of memory B cells that are specific for the conspecific neutralizing epitopes of gp41 and gp120.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the memory B cell response is broader than the circulating Ab response.
the breadth of the B cell response to HIV-1 is underestimated when plasma Ab titers are considered in isolation.
the memory B cell compartment provides a more complete view of HIV-1-specific Ab responses than plasma, and that the B cell compartment should be included in Ab analyses of HIV-1 infection.
The main takeaway from our work is that
memory B cells are more likely to contain the breadth of Ab specificities needed for neutralization of HIV-1 than circulating Abs.
the BMem repertoire can be used to identify Ab specificities that are not readily detected in contemporaneous serum samples.

the B cell response to HIV-1 infection can be much more extensive than what we see in plasma, and that the B cell memory compartment may provide a more accurate reflection of the breadth of Ab reactivity than the plasma.
